speakeroldname: Hon. R. C. MATTHEWS (Minister of National Revenue) moved:
speechtext:
That a message he sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours that this house disagrees with their amendments to Bill No. 89, an act to amend and consolidate the Excise Act. for the following reason, namely:
That the said amendments do not fully assure protection to the revenues of the crown.
And that the clerk of the house do carry the said message to the Senate.
He said: In making this motion, I would like to say that in my opinion the effect of the amendment made by the Senate would be to give to the owner, and not only to the owner but also to anyone who holds a mortgage, charge or lien upon a vehicle or thing seized as forfeit to the crown for a breach of this act the statutory right to have the forfeiture set aside in his favour. It may appear to be a hardship that an owner or lien holder should lose his property or his interest in a seized vehicle because the vehicle has been put to an illegal use by somebody else, but it has been found from long experience that in the enforcement of revenue laws and laws for the protection of public property it is necessary to have some such principle recognized. It is recognized in other acts of this parliament, for example, the Customs Act, the Fisheries Act, the Fisheries Protection Act, and the Opium and Narcotic Drugs Act. It is also, I am informed, the law in Great Britain and in most, if not all, of our own provinces. The remedy for hard cases is administrative remission which can always be arranged when it appears to be in the public interest. It is felt that the principle embodied in the proposed amendment should not be accepted by this house. It would be giving notice to all concerned that a vehicle owned by somebody else or subject to a lien can be used for illegal purposes with complete impunity.

Mr. Speaker, despite all that the minister has said, if the vehicle of an innocent party happens to be used by a third party and a seizure is made of the vehicle the only way in which the owner can recover his property is through the leniency of the departmental officials themselves or by an action in the exchequer court, and my hon. friend the minister knows full well that the exchequer court sits very seldom in the outlying provinces. All that this amendment which has been made by the Senate does is to ensure that action may be taken in a superior court

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is much more than that.
Let me put it this way, that action may be taken in the courts of the province in which the seizure is made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not the matter about which the difficulty arises at all.
Surely some protection should be given to an absolutely innocent party. From the statement of the minister himself, I gather that no attention is being paid to that matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Oh, yes.

I fail to discover it. I have a case in mind which happened in Saskatchewan. Before going away a father left explicit directions that his automobile should not be used by his son. In some way the son secured a key to the car and took it out. Along with some of his friends or with those who happened to go with him, a bottle of liquor was found in the car by the mounted police. This happened four years ago and up to date the father has not been able to recover possession of his car which is still in the hands of the department through the agency of the mounted police. Moreover, before he can take action in the exchequer court he must deposit $400. That court sits in the western provinces when there is business for it; there has been no sitting and there is not likely to be a sitting. All this has been permissible under the provisions of the Excise Act. While I am in sympathy with every facility being given to the officers of the department to take action, nevertheless there are cases of extreme hardship about which something could be done. As far as I am concerned, I do not see anything sinister in the proposal of the Senate to remedy this evil. It is an evil and it is most unfair. Surely the crown does not want to take undue advantage of a private citizen, and that is what is happening under the provisions of

Excise Act-Senate Amendments
these sections. After all, it is left pretty well to the local officer as to how he shall construe this matter. When a man in order to obtain property which is rightfully his and which has been wrongfully used against his will and consent has to refer to the procedure to which he must refer to-day, surely something is wrong and something should be done to remedy such a situation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Just a word in answer to what the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) has said. It is hoped that by bringing the matter again to the attention of their honours in the Senate, certain difficulties will be overcome. The hon. gentleman's reference to the use of the courts of the province rather than the exchequer court is a - matter to which no serious objection is made but the amendment as it stands is so at variance with all the principles that have hitherto governed in the consideration of matters of this kind. As we see it, an inducement is being offered to smugglers and those who violate the law. The principle which the Senate has asserted may be maintained but it would have to be strengthened by the addition of several subsections to the section as it stands.
I may say to the hon. gentleman that confiscation to the crown of instruments by which revenues have been defrauded is an amplification of the oldest principle which we have in our laws. In fact, it goes back to beyond the time when we had institutions at all. In our own country it is founded upon principles which were laid down in Holy Writ and in the early days of another dispensation. It is true that it is extremely difficult completely to differentiate between the innocent and guilty but it has been found in practice that unless the provision of forfeiture to the crown exists, those who disobey the law look upon perjury as a very simple thing when compared with the offence which they themselves have committed. According to judicial opinion, one of the greatest evils which this country now encounters is the prevalence of perjury. Those men who commit offences look upon perjury as a small matter when compared with the offence which they have committed. They are willing to commit perjury for the purpose of carrying through their nefarious actions. We have had striking illustrations of this in western Canada. There have been the most terrible cases in which I am convinced that human life has been sacrificed for greed and gain in connection with the administration of the liquor laws. There has been an endeavour [Mr. C. A. Stewart.l
made to impair and destroy the usefulness of our institutions by providing huge sums of money for elections and other purposes. This has been so apparent that we have to have the most stringent provisions in our laws in order to meet the situation. In these days of motor cars the situation is somewhat different. Many cases such as that mentioned by the hon. gentleman have been brought forward but where you have a father and son living in the same house and the car from the home of the father has been used for illegal purposes, the question of the forfeiture of the car has never been seriously in question until this moment. Innocency is not spelled merely by a father telling his son not to use his car. If the boy took the car and knew it was to be used for an illegal purpose, then the car becomes forfeited. One leading case we had concerned a new Cadillac car which was passing from Fernie to Montana and was forfeited. This happened in Alberta and the conviction was sustained by the privy council. I am not unwilling that there should be some modification of the statutes but as it now stands it is essential that some additional provisions be inserted in order to safeguard the public interests.

Mr. Speaker, I regret I was not present during the whole of this discussion. I have some sympathy with what the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) has said although I cannot go quite as far as he does, nor can I go quite as far as the provisions of the amendments proposed by the other house. I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is quite right when he says that there must be very stringent regulations so far as smuggling is concerned. It is quite possible that if a provision was inserted in the present law whereby the rights of forfeiture were abrogated as far as the owner of an automobile or vehicle being used for smuggling, even in a small way, was concerned, that might be very much abused. From my own experience in the department I realize that there might be collusion and possibly perjury. Smugglers might be able to accomplish their purpose and yet make it appear as though they were innocent parties. This must be guarded against. While I have no desire to criticize the Department of National Revenue, a case like that mentioned by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) should not be held over for a period of four years. I think it would be possible by a conference between representatives of the Commons and the Senate to work out something whereby some of these abuses could be prevented.

Excise Act-Senate Amendments
While I am on my feet I should like to refer to another phase of this matter. I have in mind the using of an automobile in connection with the bringing in of a small quantity of cigarettes or a silk dress. Some person may be visiting Buffalo, Detroit or one of the other border cities and bring in a silk dress, a pair of shoes or two or three cartons of cigarettes. In the case of a woman, she may be wearing the shoes. I have always contended that while an automobile was being used in the smuggling operation, the automobile itself was not intended to be used for smuggling. It just happens to be the means of conveyance for bringing the person in from the United States and incidentally bringing in perhaps a carton of cigarettes, a bit of tobacco or something of that sort. In the past the department has not forfeited the vehicle in a case of this kind, although I suppose it had the power so to do under the law. That would be a most extreme application of the law. To-day-and it was the same during my incumbency-the penalty is as high as 850 or $25 on the proprietor of a vehicle being used perhaps by a passenger who might bring in one or two cartons of cigarettes. I always contended that this was an extreme application of the law, but it comes to this in the end, that the officers of that department at the border-and I think certainly at headquarters in Ottawa-should exercise a reasonable degree of common sense. That is practically what it comes to. You have to have a stringent provision in the law to provide for cases where severe action should be taken; but the minister or his deputy or the commissioner or officers at the border should be instructed to use some degree of what is usually called horse sense in the application of the law. It might be possible bo frame some modification, by conference with the Senate, whereby the situation might be eased in those cases where there is no real intention to smuggle, and I would draw a very distinct difference in cases where people are bringing in goods to be sold again as compared with the man or woman bringing in some little article which they 'happened to have bought in Buffalo or Detroit or any other border city. I would commend to the government that they consider the possibility of making some slight modification which would relieve the situation and yet not prejudice the revenues in any large way.

The suggestion that after an act has been passed instructions should be issued by the department to outside officials to exercise a certain degree of leniency or judgment is in my
opinion very wrong. I 'have had ten years' experience in enforcing the excise laws, and if I had received word from the department under which I was working, after they had passed a law and placed it in my hands to be carried out, that I should exercise leniency,
I would not have thanked the department for placing me in that position. I have had experience as a seizing officer and have done quite a bit of seizure work during my incumbency as collector of customs in New Brunswick, and very often it was quite a task for me, conscientiously speaking, to carry out the law as it stood; yet it had to be done. I could see that in the carrying out of that law great hardship was imposed upon some individuals, but I think there should be no difficulty in framing a clause of this act which would carry out the intention of the minister in his effort to prevent smuggling and at the same time to do justice in such a case as the one referred to by the hon. member for West Edmonton. In New Brunswick, under our provincial automobile laws, we have an easy method of tracing the owner or anyone who has had anything to do with a car that may be seized, because the owner cannot drive a car without first having his licence plate, his registration, and a certificate to the effect that he is owner of the car. In the next place, any member of the family who may drive that car without a certificate or authority from the Department of Public Works, indicating that he is certified to by the head of the family as one authorized by the owner of the car to drive it, is liable to punishment. Again, no one not the owner may drive a car unless he has a chauffeur's licence. I do not know what the law is in the other provinces, but by that means in New Brunswick the authorities can trace any car to the owner or any member of the family who has authority to drive it. If, as in this case, the man who took his father's car without consent had authority under the provincial law, with a certificate to drive the car, the father would be responsible. The case is a hard one and every means possible should be taken to protect the owner whose car has been taken without his consent, and to obviate the necessity of heavy legal expenses and in many instances long delays in proving ownership, as in this case. And what about a stolen car? My car is lying out in my garage at night and some individual comes along and steals it. It is an easy matter to steal a car even when it is locked, because those who know how to go about it have simply to push up a piece of wire into certain sections of the connecting links without using the key at all, so that a

Excise Act-Senate Amendments
car may be taken whether the person who steals it has the key or not. In this way a car might easily be stolen and used for smuggling purposes and I, the owner, knowing nothing about it, after the car has been used for smuggling and has been seized by the department, find myself without the use of that car. There should be some means whereby I can reclaim the car without having to go to heavy legal expense and without having to wait two or three years to recover the car.

If anything like that
happens to my hon. friend he will have his car back immediately.

It may be all right for me, but some poor devils have to wait two or three years for it, and that is what I want to avoid. The trouble in the past has been in rectifying these errors and in trying to alleviate injury consequent upon a strict enforcement of the law by the officials. I say, however, stand by your officials when you place a law in their hands and ask them to exercise their judgment. Their judgment may be at fault, but, I say, always stand by the officials and find some means of rectifying any injustice done. That stand I take on behalf of the officials because I have been one myself and have had to suffer from a strict enforcement of laws of this kind, both in conscience and otherwise. I feel that anything the department can do to help the officials should be done. But instructions should not be issued to officials -to use their judgment and leniency; when a law of this kind is placed in their hands the officials are supposed to exercise it to the letter.

I happen to be acquainted with the case referred to by the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) and the facts are a little stronger even than he put them. The facts are these. On May 15, 1932, a certain gentleman who resides in the district I represent, the owner of an Essex sedan automobile, being obliged to go away for a week, left instructions with his wife that the son should not be allowed to use the car, and the ignition key Was placed in her possession. When this man returned he learned that his son had taken the car on May 16, without permission, and notwithstanding that his mother had forbidden him to do so. On May 15, 1932, the son took the car at the request of a friend and went to Verigin. On arrival there, he met another friend who asked for a drive to Kamsack and the son allowed this friend to get into the front seat of the car. He was then requested by another man to give him

a ride to Kamsack, which he agreed to do on that man agreeing to buy a gallon of gasoline. They then drove to a gasoline filling station. When this third man requested a drive to Kamsack, the son had no knowledge that he or anyone else in the car had any spirits or liquor of any kind and no arrangements were made that any liquor should be brought into the car by the third man or any other person and neither the son nor his friend first mentioned had any liquor on their persons or in the car. While the car was parked in front of the gasoline station a constable came along and searched the car. The third man who had a bottle of illicit liquor on him had hid it under the car where it was found, and the car was seized. That man has been without his car for three years; he has taken action in the exchequer court and has deposited $400 but that court will not meet in Saskatchewan until some time late this fall. H he has to wait until the exchequer court decides whether the car was illegally seized, he will be three years without the use of his car. I was wondering whether the Prime Minister in view of the statement just made about adopting equal jurisdiction of the superior court and the exchequer court in this matter would suggest another amendment that actions pending before the exchequer court have the privilege of being referred to the superior court.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I shall see that when the matter is being considered with the Senate that view will also be put forward.
I thank the right hon. gentleman.

Just one suggestion. It might
be well to adopt the same practice as prevails in the United States where, I am told, their citizens are allowed to bring in goods from Canada to the value of around $100. Why not insert such a provision in our law?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Successive governments
have looked into that and declined to do it for reasons that are clear; it would involve millions of dollars in revenue.
Make it $50.
Motion agreed to.

The house resumed from Wednesday, June 27, consideration of the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) for the third reading of Bill No. 19, to incorporate the Bank of Canada, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Woodsworth.

Bank oi Canada-Mr. Woodsworth

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to enter into any lengthy discussion.

The hon. member for
Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) proposed an amendment before the house adjourned last night. The motion is that the bill be read a third time. It was moved in amendment by Mr. Woodsworth:
That the bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that they have power to amend same so as to safeguard the sovereignty of parliament over Canada's financial policy.
I find that the amendment is out of order for this reason, that it is irrelevant. The sovereignty of parliament cannot be affected by the passage of a bill in this house. The sovereignty of parliament is created and defined by the British North America Act, section 91 of which states that it shall be lawful for the parliament of Canada to make laws in relation to all matters except those assigned to provincial legislatures and in the classes of subjects enumerated there are included "banking, incorporation of banks, and the issue of paper money." The sovereignty of parliament can be affected only by an amendment to the British North America Act. This amendment is therefore out of order.

Mr. Speaker, the position taken in this comer of the house on financial reform is well known. We have for years past taken the stand that we should do everything possible to obtain a stable currency and credit system.

Mr. Speaker, I think I had the floor when the house adjourned last night. With regard to the point of order it is not my intention to challenge the ruling of the Speaker. I feel that process only delays the house although I would point out that there is an open question before us as to whether the sovereignty of the house may not be destroyed, but I suppose ultimately that question could be settled only in the courts. It is, however, becoming apparent-
May I interrupt my hon. friend? He says "the sovereignty of the house." His resolution reads "the sovereignty of parliament." We are beginning to see that there is a difference between the two.
I did not quite catch my right hon. friend's remark.

My hon. friend in speaking just now used the expression "the 74726-277
sovereignty of the house", but his amendment relates to the sovereignty of parliament, I agree with him that the sovereignty of this house is being affected materially by many measures which are being put through but the sovereignty of parliament will remain what it is.

I am not going to go into this technical constitutional question. I believe the sovereignty of this house is not being safeguarded and also the sovereignty of parliament is not being safeguarded. There is, of course, a difference between the two. I shall go a little further and say that the sovereignty of the people of this country is not being safeguarded. But it seems to me it is not necessary to go into every little technical constitutional matter when one is discussing a general principle.
The house is being placed in a rather peculiar position by the decisions of the Speaker. It appears that no general resolution of this kind is permissible on third reading. It appears further that no definite amendment is permissible on the very general grounds that it might involve expenditure of money. Some of us would very definitely deny that the making of this institution a public bank would in any way interfere with His Majesty's revenues. I should have been delighted indeed to support the amendment as it was finally drafted by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie). If, however, we are not going to have the opportunity of moving any amendments, I suppose we have to let the public know that and to leave the matter as it is.
In connection with this bill I may say that I have left the matter very largely to my colleagues who were members of the committee on banking and commerce but I should like to take this last opportunity of saying a few words in regard to the situation. Perhaps I should congratulate the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) on his growing recognition of the danger of the money power. I hope he is really recognizing that danger. As a matter of fact, I am afraid he is simply repeating some phrases. I am delighted, however, to have those phrases coming from him because this marks a very decided change of attitude. For years we in this corner have advocated a central bank, one publicly owned and controlled. I regret that we were not able to place our position definitely before the country by means of an amendment to the third reading of the bill.
On the second reading I spoke strongly in favour of public ownership and control. In-



Bank of Canada-Mr. Woodsworth
deed I went so far as to say that I thought if the matter came to a vote I should have to vote against the measure. I still feel the same way. In setting up this Bank of Canada we have the opportunity to make it a public institution, and to extend the power of parliament into the realm of finance, but the government is determined that this course shall not be taken. I regret it exceedingly. It is true that certain amendments to the bill have been made in committee; I think these are all to the good, although I suggest that they are not fundamental and do not go far enough to alter the principle of the bill. I have listened to what the Prime Minister had to say but I have not been at all convinced. He pointed out the danger of political pressure; I would say there is much more danger of irresponsible class power. He speaks of appointing a sound governor. That means a man who can be trusted to carry out the behests and policies of the leaders of finance. The Prime Minister believes in having this governor practically independent of public opinion; I think that is a very dangerous proceeding. It is true that to a very large extent in the past the leaders of finance have been independent of public opinion, and I think that is the situation to-day. The trouble with this bill is that it frankly legalizes that situation. We are putting power that should belong to the sovereign people into the hands of private and irresponsible individuals. I quite recognize that the Prime Minister may not realize the danger of this situation. He himself has always moved with wealthy men-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. he hasn't.

In my judgment
he has distinctly the class consciousness of wealthy people, he accepts their point of view and their policies. He is probably firmly convinced that these are in the interests of the country at large. Some of us must challenge that position. We believe that the interests of financial men are not the interests of the public at large. We believe that it is because the country has been at their mercy that we have got into the position that we are in to-day, and that it is only as a sovereign people can make its will effective that we can hope for any remedy of the present situation. I would suggest that the Prime Minister's argument goes altogether too far. K carried out his doctrine would undermine democratic government. If he cannot trust the people, does he think he can trust someone who is altogether removed from the control of the people, or even from the pressure of public opinion? I think too

highly of the people themselves, of the ultimate good common sense of the people when their own welfare is really at stake and they are roused to actual conditions, to accept that viewpoint. The Prime Minister might . as well proceed frankly to set up a dictatorship, not merely in the realm of finance but in parliament. If the people are not able to judge of financial matters, that is the fundamental principles in finance, I cannot see how they are able to judge of the fitness of individuals to represent them in parliament or the fitness of a government to maintain its administrative powers.
The Prime Minister speaks of the difficulties in making appointments. He says that consideration must be given to race, to religion, to residence, to political affiliations, to occupation and so on. I wonder if that argument does not carry him altogether too far. We have at the present time a very capable deputy minister of finance; I wonder whether questions of race and religion and occupation entered into the consideration when he was appointed. I hope not. I cannot see why they should enter any more into the appointment of a governor of the Blank of Canada. Had I time I might take the different departments, a number of them in charge of very capable deputy ministers. Does the Prime Minister mean to infer that questions of race and religion and political allegiance and so on were at the basis of the appointment of those men, and for that reason we cannot trust them? I think that is going altogether too far. It is a decided reflection upon people to-day in public office. If our politics have been corrupt in the past, if in the past there has been altogether too much political influence of the wrong kind, surely the way out is to give scope for political influence of a better kind, to have an educated public opinion exercising its influence; not to have whole areas of public business removed altogether from the control of the people.
It is a practical question for some of us as to how to vote when the amendments are at last disposed of. I frankly admit that in a matter of this kind one could justify a vote either in the affirmative or in the negative. I believe, as indicated by the amendment which I attempted to move, that this bill does not safeguard the sovereignty of this house or of parliament. On the other hand I suggest that finance is a realm in which the people have never had sovereignty. Finance has always been aside from and superior to parliament. I think it has always dominated parliament. Theoretically parliament has been supreme, but in practice the financial kings have always dominated the

Bank of Canada-Mr. Spencer
political kings. There is no doubt whatever in my mind as to that. So, since we never have had sovereignty, I suppose we are none the worse off because this bill does not give us sovereignty. In the past we have often had conflicts between church and state, it is needless to enter into that question to-day. Now we have reached the conclusion that there is a realm in which the church is sovereign, and another realm in which the state is sovereign. In Japan, I believe, it has always been conceded that the state as constituted was never supreme over the military autocracy. The military class have been quite independent of the representative institutions of the country. There is something parallel to that in our attitude towards financial affairs. The representatives of the people through the centuries have gradually acquired power over certain realms of our life, but over the financial realm, which is so important, so vital, they have no power whatever. I would say that some of these days we will simply have to challenge the position of the financial interests or they will completely dominate our public life. That dominance undoubtedly has not been challenged in the bill before us.
Then, perhaps there is another consideration which may come in. Personally I am not anxious to give the present government too much authority. It is possibly quite true that the governor of a bank may be trusted just about as much as the present government in connection with the administration of financial affairs. I do not know that there would be much difference in policy. However, that ought not to affect one's decision in a matter of this kind. We hope that some of these days there will be in authority a government which will be in a better position to administer the financial affairs of the country.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, when I rose to speak a few moments ago I did not know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) had the floor. Needless to say I willingly gave way to him. For many years hon. members in this corner of the house have supported a stable currency and credit system. When we look back to the period between 1926 and 1929 and realize that during that
Bank of Canada-Mr. Spencer

time no less than $635,000,000 of new money was put into the money flow of this country, one appreciates that not only was trade improving, but in the event of a sudden reaction things would be very bad indeed. Then we find that in the deflation period between 1929 and 1933 there was no less than $704,000,000 written out of existence. One has to appreciate that that is one of the real reasons why we have had such a drop in prices. It is because we are up against these great differences, and these extremes of inflation and deflation that hon. members in this corner of the chamber have consistently advocated a stable currency and credit system. We have also taken the stand, as the records as far back as 1923 will show, that we believe our money system should be based on goods and services, and not upon gold. That being so we have consistently fought the idea that we should be handicapped for the sake of not having what some people think is a sufficient gold basis on which to base our monetary system.
I should like also to remind the house that we have not made proper use of our national credit. While from year to year, with our possibilities for production, we have become richer, we have actually curtailed national improvements. When we found it advisable to construct public works of different descriptions we should have been in a position to use our national credit. Only a few years ago the amount of $50,000,000 was struck out of the estimates for public works, having in mind the idea that such a saving would be one of the solutions towards bringing back prosperity. To-day I am very pleased to find that the government has realized it can make use of the national credit, and in the legislation proposed last week by the Prime Minister on behalf of the Minister of Finance we find we are going to have the sum of $40,000,000 put into public works of different kinds, without any interest cost to the nation. I claim that procedure should have been adopted years ago. The Prime Minister admits he could use $100,000,000 in that way. I take the stand that wherever there is a public work to be done, one which is needed for the public benefit, it should be done without interest charge. I contend, further, that so long as there are public works needed we should not have a pair of idle hands in the country. Such action would have the effect of cutting down the debt burden of our country, because up to the present time we have entered upon public works programs through the medium of creating debt, and such debt is creating one of the greatest burdens we have to face.

Believing along the lines I have indicated I take this opportunity of moving, seconded by Mr. Coote:
That the bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that they have power to amend so as to provide a stable currency and credit system based on goods and services, limited only to the needs of industry and social services and not by gold; to make available the national credit at cost for governmental services, and so lighten the terrific burden of debt.
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) ; Mr. Speaker, I think the amendment is out of order. The only point that I think the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) has overlooked is this, that you may amend the third reading of a bill by moving that it be not now read a third time, or you may vote against the bill being read a third time, which negatives the motion and precludes it being brought up again the same session, and lastly, if you do undertake to send the bill back to a committee to be amended it must be specifically indicated in the amendment what it is proposed to do in the way of a new or amended section. I think the hon. gentleman will agree when he has read over his amendment that he has covered everything that could well be thought of but that he has not indicated just what amendment might be made for the purpose of enabling a committee to pass upon it. In *other words, the committee has to go to work and draft a new bill. Now that is not the purpose of a third reading amendment.

Bank of Canada-Mr. Lapointe

Speaking to the point of order, Mr. Speaker, when I sat in my seat and heard four other amendments ruled out of order, each one drawn in a different way with the object of trying to get a vote of this house upon it, I rather anticipated that mine would meet with the same fate. I am not going to question your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I am only sorry that we cannot find an amendment that is acceptable to both sides of this house.

Mr. Speaker, with many of the arguments of my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) as to the sovereignty of the House of Commons and parliament I would heartily agree, but when he attempted to deliver a lecture to hon. gentlemen on this side of the house, coupled with his arguments, I would remind him that perhaps if we had had his cooperation and that of his group on other measures which have passed the house this session, and which were just as much against the sovereignty of parliament and the House of Commons, we *might have achieved better success. May I refer particularly to the peace, order and good government clause in the Unemployment Relief Act? I admit that my hon. friend voted with us on that but he had a very limited influence with his group because apart from the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) they all voted with the government and against the sovereignty of parliament and the House of Commons.
I think my hon. friend himself and all the other members of his group also voted against the amendments which were proposed from this side of the house to the marketing bill with regard to the sovereignty of parliament. I do not want to blame my hon. friend but I think he might refrain from delivering lectures to us in that respect.
But I rose particularly to say a word about section 24 of this bill and the amendment I moved in committee of the whole to that section. The government then took the amazing attitude that they would stand or fall by their proposals with regard to the issuing of notes, that they would resign if a majority of the house would consider it better that the notes of the Bank of Canada should bear English and French words instead of the notes being issued in two sets, one in English and one in French. Following that intimation the committee gave a decisive vote against my amendment. I do not propose to offer it again because that would merely give another opportunity to say that t was acting from political motives.
But I think I owe it to the principles I have upheld and to myself to say a word in answer to what I believe were the uncalled-for insinuations of the Prime Minister in his speech in answer to me. How he could say that I was violating the constitution I am at a loss to understand. He. himself said that he stood for equality. That was the purpose of my amendment; that was the principle on which it was based.
How he could say, further, that I and those who think as I do were trying to coerce or dominate the majority is still more fantastic. I took the trouble to say that I was pleading with the majority in order that they might be persuaded that the mode that I was offering was preferable to the other. Was that coercion? Was that a dominating spirit? Why should not the matter be discussed without diverting the discussion in another direction? And, Mr. Speaker, I think nobody has a right to describe me anywhere as being unreasonable and a sort of firebrand. I have tried all my life to preach Canadian unity and Canadian brotherhood in Canada, in all the provinces and in both languages, and if Providence gives me strength I propose to do so during the remaining years of my life. I repeat, why should not this matter be discussed without the use of abusive and threatening language?
Let me only say this in conclusion. Canada will continue growing and developing along sound Canadian lines. Canada and Canadians are bigger and better and more lovable than some of those who assume sometimes to speak for them. When both the Prime Minister and myself have disappeared the principles of good will upon which Canada has been built will continue to be upheld, and I hope will continue to be accepted by Canadians, and the country will advance along sound national lines.

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 123, to amend the Loan Companies Act.
He said: This bill endeavours to provide, so far as this parliament can, that the corporate powers of companies shall not be exercised where the rates of interest are larger than those they are entitled to exact by their act of incorporation. It has a retroactive effect because it applies to all companies heretofore as well as hereafter incorporated and leaves to parliament the right to decide what the maximum that may be charged shall be; and a charge in excess of that rate would result in the forfeiture by the company of its powers, there being undoubted jurisdiction in this parliament to provide that, as a condition of granting corporate existence to any group of men, it shall also follow that if they depart from the conditions imposed as to rates they may charge, forfeiture of their corporate powers shall ensue. With respect to provincial companies, that difficulty would be overcome, except to this extent, that so far as we have power, and of course we have considerable in the way of affording them recognition or dealing with them as such, they would forfeit any rights to protection from the dominion.

The house resumed from Tuesday, June 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stewart (Leeds) for the second reading of Bill No. 113, to provide for the construction and improvement of certain public works and undertakings throughout Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this bill has for its purpose the construction and betterment of certain public works enterprises throughout the dominion. With the title of the bill hon. members on this side of the house can be in accord, because it expresses a worthy purpose. However, if we look into the details and examine the schedules we find that it is designed more to meet the ends of the government of the day and might be described as a bill to advance Tory interests in this country. It is intended to be put into force in order to help the government in the next general election. It is intended, through the bill, to relieve unemployment and, to a certain extent, it is called an unemployment relief measure. If in the speeches delivered some time ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), and by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) who, during the course of his several addresses in the country and to this house has told us that unemployment is past, that we are on the upgrade, and that things are getting better, we were given the facts, then apparently this program would not be needed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will have to withdraw that statement. At no time did I say that unemployment was past.
Well, if the Prime Minister states that he did not say unemployment was past certainly he indicated to the country that unemployment was on the downgrade.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

I will withdraw it. But after the utterances by members of the government and by the Prime Minister himself I think I am safe in saying we were given to understand that the worst is over, that unemployment is on the downgrade, that business generally is going on in greater proportions, and that we may expect a return to greater activity very soon.
Hear, hear.

If these statements are true, and if the government states they are true, then the country can stand on its own fMr. Bennett.]
feet, and I do not think these public works would be necessary in all places. May I point out that in the years 1929, 1930 and since requests were made to the Department of Public Works and to the government by the constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay for certain works which were absolutely necessary. I hold in my hand a copy of the votes and proceedings of this house for May 17, 1933, in which I find certain questions credited to me. These questions were asked regarding certain works at Pentecote River, Aux Coudres Island, Mutton Bay, Moisiei Magpie, Longue Pointe du Mingan, Harrington Harbour, Hamilton Cove on the Portneuf river, Dolbeau, Betsiamites, Beaupre, Richers Bay, Petites Bergeronnes, Point-au-Boisvert, Point Lebel, Port-au-Persil, Port-au-Saumon, Riviere-aux-Vases, River Blondelle, St-Anne de Beaupre, a retaining wall on the St-Jean river, work on the St-Margaret river, a wharf at St-Irenee, the building of a post office at Pointe-au-Pic and works at St-Simeon, Sept-Iles, Sheldrake, Baie St-Paul and Petite Riviere St-Francois.
All these works I have just mentioned are absolutely necessary now, and were necessary in 1930, 1931, 1932 and 1933. I am pleased that this amount has been provided for the work at that place. If those moneys had been spent they would have given a great deal of work to the unemployed people in the vicinity of Murray Bay, where there is a large pulp and paper mill and where, for the last three years, the people have been out of employment.

Mr. Speaker, according to the 1931
census there are 44 cities and 347 towns in Canada. By this bill the towns 'have not received consideration proportionate to that given to the larger cities. The population of the various towns in Alberta is 34,042 while the population of the cities is 194,203. The population of both towns and cities totals 228,245. The total population of Alberta is 731,605 and subtracting the population of the towns and cities, leaves a population of 503,360 in the villages and upon the farms. I could supply the figures for the other provinces 'but I understand at this late stage there is at least a moral time limit upon our speeches. Therefore, I shall not take up the time of the house by quoting these various statistics. For every person living in the towns of Canada there are no more than six living in the cities. As these expenditures are allocated, all that Alberta will get is $150,000 for a post office and administration building at Banff, $1,200,000 for barracks in Calgary, $200,000 for Royal Canadian Mounted Police barracks in Edmonton, and $7,400 for a telephone line from Keg river to Carcajou. It is on behalf of those who live in the small towns that I speak to-day. I will speak for the farmers later. A member on the other side said that some of the money to be expended on these barracks in Calgary might easily be transferred to his district in Gaspe or the, town in which he lives; I forget what he said. Well, I might say that at least $50,000 of this money could easily be transferred to the town of Vegre-ville where we have police, headquarters, because these men have absolutely no housing. I would therefore ask the minister if at all possible to reconsider this vote so that some of the towns in our province might come in on the allocation of these expenditures.
Take the maritime provinces. There are only about a million people there, and not only from what I have heard from members from that part of the country, but from' what I have read in newspapers and magazines, they are not suffering from the depression as we are in the west. In the three prairie provinces we have 2,350,000 people as compared with a little over 1,000,000 in all the maritimes; yet the maritimes have received $5,000,000 whereas the province of Alberta

receives only $1,700,000. The maritimes are receiving $100,000 more than the three prairie provinces put together. In conclusion I do not think I can do better than quote to the house the views of the various chambers of commerce in the west regarding the allocation of these expenditures so far as the small towns are concerned. Here is a resolution passed in a very large district in Alberta:
Whereas the effects of the depression have been equally disastrous to all classes of urban communities, in that many of the smaller centres have a relief burden as great (on a per capita basis), as the largest cities;
And whereas the tax-paying ability of the residents of much smaller centres has become seriously impaired because of depressed business conditions;
And whereas the people of the dominion, regardless of place of residence, w'ill indirectly pay for any national program of works that may be instituted:
Be it therefore resolved, that we, the boards of trade and chambers of commerce of north eastern Alberta in conference assembled at Vegreville, this 15th day of January, 1934, petition the government of the dominion and province respectively, as follows:
1.	That any program of public works be so framed as to afford relief from the unemployment burden to all classes of urban municipality alike.
2.	That any such program be of a nature to be of lasting benefit to the province generally and be designed to create buying power and debt paying ability in the smaller as well as the larger centres.
3.	That employment on any works instituted as a part of the national program be afforded to unemployed on the basis of merit only, and without reference to former domicile. Provided, however, that this condition shall not apply, should the municipality in which the work is instituted share in the cost thereof to the extent of at least 33J per cent.
One hon. member to my right said that these moneys should have been expended four years ago. I might add that something of this sort should have been done in 1930 but was not. I believe that more money could be expended, but I certainly do think that some of it should have been allocated to the smaller places-at least more than has been given. I therefore appeal to the minister to do something for the smaller towns.

No doubt the people of Canada have been looking forward to the introduction of this bill ever since the announcement was made early in the winter that such a measure would be brought down. We need better homes for the working class and some of this money could be used for that purpose to far better advantage and more in the interests of the Canadian people than for the building of armouries and mounted police barracks. There are fifteen hundred cases of tuberculosis in Vancouver. Two new cases occur every day, and as many as a hundred and twenty cases were found' in one month this year.
^One death occurs every forty-eight hours in Vancouver from the disease, which is causing six times as many deaths here as all other infectious diseases together.
Then he goes on to say:
Doctor Hatfield went on to describe the sad plight of men released from tuberculosis treatment but unable to compete on the labour market immediately. Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay
the house very much in discussing this bill; however, in the interest of my constituency I intend to make a few comments. There are small towns in rural counties. For instance, we have in the county of Terrebonne, the town of St. Jerome with 10,000 population; the towns of St. Therese, Terrebonne and St. Agathe, where I have the honour to reside. during the last three years of the crisis, had to provide for the needs of a great number of unemployed by carrying out certain undertakings with the help of both dominion and provincial governments. Many unemployed-the majority of them-are neither bricklayers, carpenters nor masons, but are purely and simply navvies or labourers. Moreover, sir, we have in counties like the one I have the honour to represent, the advantage of being able to carry on certain work in the forests. No doubt this measure will somewhat improve the sad plight in which the workmen of Montreal and those of all large cities in Canada find themselves at present.

I trust that no political distinction will be made in distributing the work among those who request it, secondly, wages not only rational but substantial should be paid to them. Many unfair, unjust, I may even say vile acts take place at present under the plea of so called rational wages. I therefore request as an appendage to this bill, not only rational but substantial wages, to which all workmen are rightly entitled. Moreover, I equally request that tenders be the rule laid down in regard work calling for even a smaller outlay than $25,000.
There are in our large cities a considerable number of smal| contractors who, in the past, have contributed more to help the workmen and to increase public wealth than those large companies which operating here and there, whose shareholders are foreigners and managers do not understand the mentality of our workers. These small contractors have had, within the last few years, material lying idle and it is high time that the government allow these people, who have made enormous losses since the beginning of the crisis, not only to utilize their material but to give work to the men they employed in the past.
There is another matter which I want to point out: The hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) insisted the other day in the course of his speech, that the material utilized in these various enterprises should be Canadian in order that this bill should afford still more work to those who in this country have been idle for a number of years.

This measure, I stated a moment ago, will not afford the complete relief expected. What will become of our white shirt employees? What will become of our former office employees? What will become of our youth?

The white shirt employees can become bookkeepers.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation):	The white
shirt employees cannot become bookkeepers?

They are clerks.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation):	The present
bill will require bookkeeping, but this work will be performed by the employees of large companies, so that our white shirt people will find very little comfort in the suggestion of my hon. friend.
You have just referred to small contractors.

They are all
"cimenteurs" (such liars or cement workers).
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): ' Instead of so often interrupting those who take more interest than he does in endeavouring to relieve the depression existing in our rural districts, the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge would be more deserving of praise, if following the example of the Liberal members who spoke just now, he championed oftener in the house the interests of his county.
I shall be brief, sir. It is very fine to present to workers a measure of this kind so as to deceive them, but-I am addressing myself to the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-is he or would he be following the example of his government, in favour of cutting out the dole? I state that the dole- necessity is law at present-must still be continued after this act is put into force. It is futile to think for a moment of cutting out the dole, let it be a joint contribution by the dominion government, provincial governments and our cities. I am in favour of continuing the dole, recognizing, with all those endowed with some practical sense, the impossibility, through a bill like this one, of affording a complete solution to the sad unemployment problem. And that, sir, is my last word.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister if he has been informed as to the deplorable condition of the harbour at Whitby, county of Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, on several occasions representations have been made as to the necessity for dredging at

Public Works Construction-Mr. Ferland
Whitby. The general vote is in terms sufficiently elastic to permit that work to be done, if we conclude that it should be done.
No definite answer yet.
Have I the assurance of the minister that the matter is under contemplation?
We are not in committee.
The hon. member may have the assurance of the minister that what he has said to-day will be considered, and the situation at Whitby reviewed.

I would not press the matter were it not for the fact that this bill has been staged as a relief measure. There are unemployed in Whitby. It has been pointed out by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) that the majority of the undertakings are for non-productive purposes.
I regret the action of the government in spending so much money on such non-productive purposes. May I associate myself with the statement or warning of the leader of the opposition as to the dangers of inflation. However, since the measure is for non-productive purposes, since it is to be financed out of money drawn from the clouds and since we have unemployed in Whitby I would ask that this bill should provide that the unemployed in Whitby may be set to work on the improvement of the Whitby harbour.
Mr. CHARLES E. FERLAND (Joliette) (Translation):	A number of speakers, sir,
who preceded me in this debate have in one way or another apologized for taking part in the discussion, stating that their intention was to be brief. There are so many things to say about this bill that I shall immediately state that I shall take the necessary time to make my remarks. The bill under consideration had for a long time been promised to us. It was announced with much flurry and exaggeration during the election campaign of 1930, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and his followers promised to settle the unemployment question. Let us examine the promises of this session; for many months we have been promised this bill to relieve unemployment. A few weeks ago our scrupulous Prime Minister stated that he could not introduce this bill before the elections of Ontario and Saskatchewan for fear of influencing the people's vote. I now realize that he was perfectly right. In fact it would have influenced the people. The constituencies set aside in this bill are numerous; there are many needs for which the bill 74726-2781
should have provided, yet they were ignored Had this measure been brought down previous to the Ontario election, there can be no doubt that the poor candidates of Ontario would have had the same fate as those of Saskatchewan, who failed to elect one of their candidates. The Prime Minister feared to harm the chances of the Conservative candidates and that is why he did not wish to embarrass them.
If we consider the bill, on the whole, we find that certain features must be examined. Its object is to relieve unemployment. Therefore, it must provide work wherever there are unemployed. What do we find in this bill? There are in Quebec about 1,400 municipalities. How many are included in this measure? Can any one find more than twenty-four? Among these twenty-four a number have no unemployment problem. Thus, for instance, I could point out to the little municipality of Valois, in the county of Jacques Cartier where, to my knowledge, no unemployed are to be found, but where, however, an expenditure of $25,000 is authorized.
What characterizes this bill, is the total disregard for farmers in centres half urban and half rural, as in the case of the county of Joliette. In cities like Joliette or St. Hyacinthe, and those of the importance of Sherbrooke or Riviere du Loup or in so many other cities of Quebec, where there are so many unemployed, it was an easy matter to provide for public works which would at the same time have helped the farmers. There are many public buildings which could have been erected in such cities. As the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Parent) also pointed out, a moment ago, many of such undertakings could have relieved the unemployed, even outside of cities. For instance, if one examines the present situation in the northern parts of the counties of Joliette, Berthier Maskinonge, 1'Assomption, Montcalm and Terrebonne, one may note that many farmers cannot depend any longer on their land for a livelihood because the returns are insufficient, although in the past the land was profitable and the farmers were comfortably off. There are public works which could be carried out in those northern sections; roads to be built in the county of Joliette, as well as in the county of Berthier-Maskinonge represented by a member who was able to obtain for the town of Berthier a post office which will cost about $48,500.
The government could and should have appropriated for such works a larger amount, since it is an easy task for them to finance
4400	_	COMMONS
Public Works Construction-Mr. Ferland
undertakings of this nature in a country whose credit, are we to believe our friends in the government, is greater than that of all other nations. The government could have provided for certain undertakings which would have given practical and profitable results to farmers. At the inquiry on the spreads of price and mass purchasing, the disadvantages of tobacco trusts were investigated and it was pointed out to the government that the tobacco growers of Quebec especially those of the counties of Joliette, L'Assomption, Montcalm and Berthier-Maskinonge can no more find markets for their products which they have to sell at exceedingly low prices, a few cents per pound. At a sitting of the committee, the mayor of St. Jacques-l'Achigan, Mr. Joseph Marion, brought out a very interesting memorandum which contained suggestions made by tobacco growers of my district in order to remedy this disastrous and ruinous situation. It concludes as follows at page 1682 of the report:
Our suggestions greatly resemble those made by the Ontario tobacco growers: organization of the official grading through the means of a central warehouse for drying, grading and public auctioning.
The government should have provided for a central warehouse for drying, grading and selling by public auction, in our important district. While giving work, to the unemployed in our district, it should also have provided for cold storage plants for the farmer's perishable products in order, to complete the work undertaken by the co-operative associations of butter-dairies and farm industry products. Perishable commodities could be stored in these plants, such as butter, when, during a few months in the year, prices are low or when there is over production. One could store in those plants, for the time being, the maple products which are marketed without being graded or carefully selected and sacrificed at ruinous prices, while a local market is being flooded with large quantities of this commodity, far more than required by the local population.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Will
the hon. member allow me to ask him a question? Does he not think that the Marketing of Natural Products Act will permit exactly what he suggests?
I regret, sir, that I have to reply in the negative, because I have no faith in the results of the act to which my hon. friend, the Minister of Marine ''Mr. Duranleau) has just referred.
To be saved, one must have faith.
Faith will remove mountains.
Am I to understand that the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Barrette) has no faith himself in that act?
I did not make that statement. I am quite confident on the contrary.
Would the hon. member repeat what I did not catch? Will he explain what he means when he states that I have no faith?
I stated that to be saved, one must have faith.

Then, I
must reply to my hon. friend that if one must have faith to be saved, I doubt very much that he has enough to save his party and government at the next election.
What also Characterizes the bill under consideration, is the particular solicitude of the government to specially favour the Quebec Counties represented in the house by Conservative members. One notes that the government paid special attention and carefully handled the matter.
That is quite natural.
To this, the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Lafleche) replies: Quite naturally.
That is natural 1
This remark is entirely in keeping with his principles, his mentality and with the policy of the Conservative party generally.
You have principles when in the opposition and then when in power, you disown them. That is the difference existing between us.

We expected that partiality in the distribution of public works in Quebec. If at least they had been distributed in all cities where there are unemployed!-And we are aware that there are unemployed in all cities. The government has not forgotten that it helped the unemployed of all cities in Quebec and that, at present, there are unemployed in all the cities which are not mentioned in the bill and which should have been included among others Sherbrooke, whose population is close on 30,000; Joliette whose population reaches almost 12,000; St. Hyaeinthe, Riviere-du-Loup.

Public Works Construction-Mr. Ferland
Those two counties are represented in the house.

-and even Hull. I find it ridiculous that the government has, not thought of helping the unemployed of Hull. If there is a city which is suffering from unemployment where the working population is at present in distress it is certainly the city of Hull. The government can certainly not close its eyes to what takes place just outside the limits of the Capital. Yet for the sole reason, obviously-if there are others, we should be told-that Hull is represented by a Liberal member, no work for the unemployed is mentioned, for this municipality, in the bill.
Why should there not be any work in the new diocese of Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm? There is no excuse for ignoring this new county, there is no reason for not affording relief to the people of this new constituency. This county has a number of parishes on the St. Lawrence river, and it could also, have benefited by the work to be undertaken in the various rivers of this country. Particularly in Quebec, a considerable amount of the money to be voted, which represents many millions of dollars, will be utilized in carrying out work on the St. Lawrence or other rivers. One might think that it is "watered stock"- electiofi watered stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Are
you opposed to the work which will be done on the St. Lawrence?

In principle, I am in favour of the work to be carried out on the St. Lawrence, but not in the way which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine wishes to distribute it.
For instance, I am opposed to spending considerable amounts, hundreds of thousands of dollars to build a concrete wall in order to prevent the embankment in the county of my hon. friend from falling into the St. Lawrence river.
It is to prevent the county from sliding away!

There is precisely in this bill a large item, $40,000 to construct a cement wall which according to the hon. Minister's statement would serve to protect another wall that cost $68,000, and also be an extension to the latter.
Especially-this is not the statement of the hon. minister-the said wall will serve to protect the government at the next election. I fear that the protection will be of no avail.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Time
will tell.
What are the undertakings you have suggested for the county of Joliette?

I suggested a number of undertakings for the county of Joliette, which could also have applied to the county of Berthier and which the hon. member forgot to request. He contented himself with a post office at Berthier. For at least three or four years past this post office has been requested. I am pleased that the hon. member has obtained it and I have no objection to there being erected at a cost of $48,000 a beautiful post office in the town of Berthier and, even, that there should be placed at the main entrance a commemorative bust of the member for Berthier who is not very tall, so that it will not take a great deal of stone, and therefore, will not cost much.
For some time past, sir, a campaign has been waged in the press so as to protest against the deplorable state of the two bridges which link Montreal to the Joliette L'Assomption-Montcalm county. As stated in the press, these bridges are truly a disgrace to the Canadian metropolis; they are in a lamentable state, paved with planks which act like an accordion when automobiles pass over them, the bridges are too narrow and have no sidewalks for pedestrians who travel daily from Charlemagne to Montreal to earn a livelihood.
These pedestrians are constantly exposed to serious accidents. It would be an easy matter to rebuild these bridges with the funds appropriated to relieve unemployment and if there be not sufficient to rebuild them, they could be repaired; the foundations could be strengthened, sidewalks could be added on each side for pedestrians and these' floating planks could be replaced by a cement floor or by some other material. However, it is quite easy to explain that the government did not think of repairing or rebuilding these bridges. The counties of Joliette and L'Assomption-Montcalm are negligible quantities for our friends opposite since they do not even want to let them keep their members and that they remove from these counties, owing to the redistribution of seats, one member out of two.
Such is, sir, the spirit of justice which animates our friends of the Conservative party. This is quite in keeping with their policy of the last few years, it is clearly written in this bill, which is also as unfair as the Redistribution Act by virtue of which there exists in Quebec rural counties that have only about 20,000 population while others have a population of 60,000. To prove
4402	COMMONS
Public Works Construction-Mr. Fontaine
my statement, that this bill is unfair and that it sets aside the Liberal counties, I have but to point out to the fact that the largest rural county of Quebec, the new county of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm has been entirely ignored, not even being mentioned.
Certain municipalities will benefit by this bill; I am very pleased. I have no objection to counties represented by Conservative members being given work; however, I state that counties having Liberal representatives should also have their share, since there are unemployed everywhere.
Chicoutimi and Father Point are in counties represented by Liberals. Lacolle is represented by a Liberal, the member for St. Johns-Tberville (Mr. Rheaume).

Lacolle has
been transferred (decode).
That does not go (colie).

The hon.
member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Lafleche) states that some counties represented by Liberals obtained work. It is true that some did; however, in most cases one finds that the reason and justification for this is very obvious. If, for instance, we take Sorel, it was necessary to authorize work in that place, since by the policy of our Conservative friends, the workers at Sorel had been dismissed so as to make place for workers from the counties of Berthier-Maskinonge, Champlain, Yamaska and other Conservative counties, The conservative electors must be taken care of and given assistance wherever they are, even if they are in Liberal counties.
I shall not insist any further, sir; I clearly showed that this bill smacks of partiality, unfairness and " partisanship " the usual policy of the government, and, although the principle of giving out work is accepted by all, I state in closing my remarks that the government is to blame for the way it distributes work.

begins his remarks, I should like to transmit to the house the following message from the deputy assistant secretary of the Governor General:
