May I also ask him whether he has had any representations from any organization in Manitoba to allow a certain amount of this money to be used in the way of guaranteeing bonds to construct a sugar beet factory in that province? If he has, why has he not given some consideration to that in these schedules? If a certain amount of money is to be spent to relieve unemployment, why should it not be spent on projects which will give employment? You construct a public building to-day and after it is erected there is a cost for its upkeep, but if certain concessions were given for the construction of, say, a sugar beet factory, that would give employment for years to come and I think the money would be better expended. I do not know whether the minister is in a position to answer me now, but if he cannot do so, I hope before he spends this money his heart will open up for the historic county of Provencher.

I am very much moved by the eloquent and patriotic appeal of my hon. friend, and I quite join with him in his appreciation of the magnificent constituency of Provencher. The insertion of an item in the estimates does not create any obligation on the part of the government to expend the money; it just makes it available for the purpose if and when the government decides that it should be so expended. My hon. friend knows very well that in 1930 the estimates for public works were very large; they were larger than I think the revenues of the country warranted, and it was found that the revenues as they came in did not

As to the building to which my hon. friend refers, I assume that it is of smaller type, and as has been said by several hon. gentlemen, that kind of construction does not contribute very much to the relief of unemployment which my hon. friend is frank enough to admit is not very severe in his constituency. Will the minister undertake to justify an expenditure under this bill to-day when he cancelled expenditures that had been voted by this house for my constituency? I do not see how he can do it. I have no quarrel with anyone who can get a public building in his riding, but the minister when he came into power cancelled the construction of buildings in my riding for which tenders had been called, yet to-day he is voting money under this schedule for works which to my mind are no more essential than those voted in 1930.

If it is any

I have no disapproval to

A little farther away. One

I decided not to say anything on the second reading of this bill because I was in favour of the principle, but now that the bill is in committee I want to draw the attention of the minister to one or two items which I think he has overlooked. I find for British Columbia three or four items specified, for Vancouver, Victoria, New Westminster and Quesnel. I call the minister's attention to the fact that on several occasions representations have been made to the government and to himself by boards of trade, by the Conservative association in northern and central British Columbia, and by myself, as to the necessity for having a federal building for that district in Prince Rupert. The building that houses the

different departments there at the present time is a barn, not fit to be called a public building, yet the federal revenue from that district is approximately $200,000 a year. The government are paying rent for the shack they occupy in Prince Rupert. I know that the minister is tired of listening to me, and the minister who represents British Columbia in the cabinet, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), is watching me and I know he is also very familiar with this story. I fail to understand the omission from this bill of any item for Prince Rupert because I know that the boards of trade and other bodies have made representations; the government of British Columbia and the premier of British Columbia have made representations to the minister as well as to the Prime Minister, showing that this is a necessary work and one that should be carried on for unemployment relief. Yet nothing has been done, and as a representative of north and central British Columbia I ask the government what voice they listen to in regard to these matters. If it be the provincial government, if it be public bodies such as chambers of commerce and boards of trade, representations have been received from them. If it is recommendations made by the representative of the constituency that they listen to, I have made such representation. If all those representations are ignored I presume the one who is heard is the minister representing British Columbia in the federal cabinet, the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I know that he has always been fair to the whole of British Columbia, not to a part only, so I fail absolutely to understand how it is that all these representations in respect to northern and central British Columbia have been entirely ignored. I might point out that while some money is appropriated for British Columbia, the Minister of Trade and Commerce knows that those works are all in the southern part of the province, hundreds of miles or as much as a thousand miles from central and northern British Columbia. Is it reasonable to expect that men who need employment are going to be sent a thousand miles to get the benefit of this work, or is something to be done for them in their own district? I realize that there is a provision of $2,000,000 for miscellaneous works under the Department of the Interior. I appreciate that the government are finding something to take the place of the dole, which I was absolutely against from the beginning. But since this work is to be distributed to help unemployment the government should give some recognition to the suggestions from public bodies that are familiar with conditions 74726-280 i
in each district. I hope that when the distribution is being made of this money for rivers and harbours and buildings in general, something like $5,500,000, the needs of northern and central British Columbia will be given consideration. I should like very much to have a few words from the minister, because I believe he will appreciate what I have said, and the representations I have made. May I have an answer?

What rather impressed
me as being a bit extraordinary was the reference the hon. member made to the building now occupied by the federal services in Prince Rupert. On one occasion he referred to them as barns, and on another occasion he called them shacks.
Yes. Both names apply.

He states now that that
is true. I recall that the government which preceded this one, and which he supported, entered into a five year lease on these buildings at a rate of about $5,000 a year, and I find it a little difficult to justify the payment of $5,000 a year for either a shack or a barn.
There must have been extenuating circumstances.

The hon. member is on the horns of a dilemma. However, I have heard what he said, and have taken note of the fact that he appealed to me as a minister representing the province of British Columbia. Obviously every place cannot be cared for. Certainly no one is putting any obstacle in the way of a building being built where he has indicated. The matter of a building for Prince Rupert will in due course receive consideration from my colleague the Minister of Public Works and from me, so far as I have anything to do with it. Why did not my hon.

In bill 113, under consideration, there are two items which particularly interest me because my constituency is situated on the south shore of the river, while a Conservative member represents the constituency on the north shore. I have much esteem for the gentleman. The following is What I find:
Champlain and Lorne Dry Docks, Que.-Repairs to buildings, caisson house, hose tower and concrete masonry, $18,000.
I also see:
Champlain Dry Docks, Que.-Keel blocks, $26,000.
This amounts to $44,000. This bill is intituled :
An Act to provide for the construction and improvement of certain public works and undertakings throughout Canada.
I am aware that the hon. member representing the constituency on the north shore has received his full share; $44,000 is being voted for his constituency. I wish to inquire of the government whether this $44,000 is included in the 40 or 50 millions appropriated to public works or whether it is included in the estimates of the Department of Marine? Moreover, whether this is a gift to the county of Champlain, exclusively .of other counties? Until I read the section of the act, I never thought that there existed a dry dock at Champlain. I was under the impression that there existed some dock to build'vessels, but as such docks could not exist everywhere, I began to wonder whether it was actually a gift so as to build a dry dock at Champlain. Is this amount included in the $40,000,000, or $50,000,000 or whether it is included in the estimates of the Marine department? Is there a dry dock at Champlain?

I am anxious to get some information from the Minister of Public Works. First of all may I say that it appears curious not only to myself but to the house and country that the government should bring at this late hour in the session a bill providing for an expenditure of $40,000,000, without giving proper time for the representatives of the people to discuss intelligently the items included in this bill. I wonder if hon. gentlemen opposite realize what $40,000,000 mean.
The hon. member is out of order.
Well, I am just coming to the items.
The hon. gentleman is entirely out of order. We are considering clause 5, administration.
We have been told by the Minister of Public Works that opportunities would be given to discuss the matter fully.
If there is unanimous consent of the committee.
No.
I am merely asking the same privilege which has been extended to other hon. members.
And further, if the committee will permit me to say so, we are discussing section 5, whereby the minister may transfer the expenditure of moneys to several departments.

With all due respect to the chair, may I continue my argument? Before proceeding to the questions I wish to ask I should like to observe that the people throughout the country think it strange that in the dying hours of a session, if not of the government itself, the representatives of the people should be asked to vote $40,000,000 to be expended upon the recommendation of a body-no matter how respectable it might be-the builders' corporation, I have been told. By the way, I should like to know if the association of builders are going to have all the contracts to be awarded under this measure. However I am not going to go too fast; we will wait and watch. Does the government realize that $40,000,000 is a very large amount of money?
Some of the people say it is not enough.

If the Solicitor General, who has just interrupted me, will take the trouble to count $40,000,000, one dollar a minute, he will find that it will take him 1,388 days to

perform his task, and by that time he will be in the opposition, or back in his office in Quebec. Hon. members on this side are interested in this discussion, and yet we have not time to discuss matters. That is why we are bound to shorten our remarks. The Minister of Public Works is aware of the fact that last year and again this year I wrote him and interviewed him about dredging the Petite Riviere Montreal. That river drams about eleven thousand acres of the best land in the country, and upon that river there has already been spent jointly by this government and the Quebec government from $29,000 to $30,000. At a time when that expenditure was about to produce its effect, this government, because the riding is a Liberal one, refused to appropriate the further amount necessary to finish the work, though only about five thousand dollars more is required. I do not see any item in the schedule for that purpose, and I very respectfully ask the minister why such an item is not there.

There is no -adequate
reason.

Furthermore, in the town of Laprairie we have a brick industry, practically the only industry in the town, but due, I will not say wholly to the policies of this government, construction in this country is at a standstill and as a consequence the brickyards in Laprairie, four in number, are idle. We have at least four hundred families in Laprairie who are without work and in a state of starvation, despite the fact that the town of Laprairie, through the provincial government, backed by the request of Conservatives in my riding, by my good friend Mr. Gustave Monet, my opponent in the last election and a very influential representative of the Conservative party in Montreal, and also through myself, requested this government to contribute to the construction of a street called Ste. Rose in Laprairie. This government has been begged to do that work for the last -two years, and only last year this government decided to build the street under its relief policy, but that was at the beginning of December when it was -too late to begin the work. I do not see any item in this schedule for -that work. It would require an expenditure of approximately $10,000, but nothing has been done.
I see a large vote in the schedule of this bill for the Interior department and for the Department of Indian Affairs. I wonder if the government has in mind the building of a water system, as the Minister of Public Works indicated a short time ago, for the Caughnawaga Indian reserve. It is a large reserve and for many years they have been asking for a water system to be built at Caugh-nawaga, -but they are still obliged to fetch their water from the river because the village of Caughnawaga is built on a rock and there are no wells from which they can get water. This work is absolutely necessary and I would ask the minister if he has any amount for that purpose.
I also see an amount under the Department of Indian Affairs for the reconstruction of Indian residential and day schools and for hospitals. The Minister of Public Works knows perfectly well that Caughnawaga is badly in need of a hospital. Is any special amount being voted for that purpose? I should like to have an answer from the minister to all of these questions.
I am sorry that the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) is not in his seat. I would like to know how so influential a member of the government has not been able to get a larger -amount for his riding. I have been told all around here that this money has been appropriated upon the influence and recommendation of friends of the government. I am surprised that a minister of the crown so near to the government has got only $40,000 for the county of Chambly, just for a dyke. What about the Chambly canal, repairs for which are so necessary that it is impossible at the present time for a boat to pass through the canal because it is pretty nearly full up, like some of the ditches in Ontario were filled up during the last election campaign, making it absolutely necessary that they should be dug out again.
I strongly protest, Mr. Chairman, against this policy which the government presents to parliament in the last hours of the session, and I also protest strongly against the government appropriating moneys where it is not needed in many cases, and appropriating nothing for many other places where there is urgent -need for public works. I am speaking not only for myself but for the people I have the honour to represent in this house, and the country as a whole I believe will resent this policy of the government, coming down and asking parliament for an appropriation of forty million dollars just to be used for electioneering purposes, and doing it in the dying days of the session after the people of this country have been waiting for four years for redress and for fulfilment of the promises which hon. gentlemen opposite made during the last election campaign. I think the people have a right to know that the government is following such a policy, and if the government.

He has pointed out that one of my -colleagues, as he says, an influential member of the government, is getting practically nothing for his constituency. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Murphy) will give an explanation in connection with that. It comes under that department and I Teally know nothing about the matter. Is it not true that the minister has received petitions asking that a contribution of one-third be made by the government for the building of that street in Laprairie due to the fact that nearly everyone in the town is unemployed?

It has been there.
Then it goes to the Department of Labour.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-Tenders.

I should like to say a word on the question of tenders. I should like to urge that where tenders are called for, especially for works which are not very large, as far as possible they should be confined to the particular locality provided there are a sufficient number of contractors of repute to ensure proper and reasonable competition. I take it that the purpose of the bill is to provide work, and I am a little bit afraid that a wide call for tenders would mean cut-throat competition and the benefits of the work would be practically nil. I suggest that in calling

for tenders for works involving $200,000 or $300,000 the invitations for tenders should be confined as far as possible to local contractors where there are a sufficient number to ensure bona fide competition.
My hon. friend has special reference to Edmonton tenders?

No, I have not. I am referring to tenders for works of a comparatively moderate character, no matter in what city they may be. If tenders are to be called for over the whole province or over two or three provinces, it will mean that the local people will not get the benefit of the work. Many local contractors have been without work for a long time and they will find that the contracts are being awarded to large contractors who have underbid. In such cases the large contractor generally brings in some of his clerks and higher paid employees from some other city. If the purpose of this bill is to provide as much benefit as possible, consideration should be given as far as possible to the local places in which the work is done.
There is another matter which I should like to emphasize, and which has been emphasized already by hon. members on both sides who have spoken. Special care should be taken to ensure that the fair wage clause is inserted, not merely in the original contract- I know it will be-but in the subcontracts as well, and that this clause is enforced in connection with all contracts. I know that in many tenders let by the government, not for construction work but for the supplying of goods, the fair wage clause is scandalously ignored. Work is being done under government contracts under conditions of practically sweated labour. The prices paid in some instances are so low that the work cannot be produced on terms of fair wages or fair working hours. I ask that special care be taken to see that these conditions are observed in connection with this relief bill.

The minister was good
enough to let me have a copy of the amendment which he proposes to move to section
7.	I had already prepared an amendment to take the place of sections 6 and 7, and I was wondering if there would be any objection to considering the two sections together.

Section 6 provides that tenders shall be invited "except as hereinafter provided." The principle of that section is absolutely sound, and it is the basis of all operations under the bill. It is what my hon. friend has been contending for. I think we should start with that prin-

ciple, that tenders are to be invited except where the governor in council decides otherwise. I believe we should retain that principle.

The minister will bear in
mind that my objection to section 6 is that the tenders are not to be publicly advertised. I think this question of tenders should be settled along the lines of the suggestion of the Prime Minister, that it should follow the provisions of the Public Works Act. Even with the amendment which my hon. friend proposes to move to section 7, I submit that the objects of the bill will be better served by putting in section 36 of the Public Works Act, which would cover both section 6 and section 7 of the bill. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot):
That sections 6 and 7 be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"6. Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works, except in cases
(a)	of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest; or
(b)	in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department, or
(c)	where the estimated cost of the work is less than five thousand dollars and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
2. Whenever in case of any work tenders are required to be or are invited, the minister having charge of the department concerned shall submit all tenders received therefor to the governor in council, and the contract for the work shall be awarded under the direction of the governor in council.
And that present sections numbered eight, nine and ten be renumbered as seven, eight and nine.
In moving that, I do not think it is necessary for me to add anything to what I said yesterday in regard to this matter. It will give us public advertisement of tenders and will do away with the necessity for the two sections 6 and 7. I understand that the minister proposes to concede, in section 7, pretty much what was advocated yesterday by other members on this side as well as by myself. I wish to say one word which I did not stress yesterday and it is partly in answer to what my hon. friend from Edmonton has said in regard to the persons from whom tenders are received. It is a pretty dangerous thing to attempt to limit the scope of the tender. In tenders for Canadian business, it seems to me that if you are going to get the best value for your money you should not attempt to limit to any one province or section the people from
whom tenders may be received. That has been the practice in the past and it is the proper policy. I believe that all the advantages suggested by my hon. friend from. Edmonton can be obtained by imposing upon whoever gets the contract the conditions that are requested with regard to the labour that shall be used upon that contract.

This amendment is not in order. We are considering section 6 and this is an amendment to section 6 and 7. Standing order 76 provides:
In proceedings in committee of the whole house upon bills, the preamble is first postponed, and then every clause considered by the committee in its proper order; the preamble and title to be last considered.
I made the suggestion, and I thought it was concurred in, that 6 and 7 be considered together.
I have been contending the very opposite, that 6 should stand on its own merits. I move that the committee rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again.

I have some further remarks to make.
Progress reported.
